h1:
Sisaket Volcanic Durian
Tasting at the Orchards of Kantharalak & Khun Han
intro: Sisaket became Isan's durian town because of the soil, plain and simple. The foothills of the Phanom Dong Rak range around Kantharalak, Khun Han and Si Rattana sit on old volcanic soil weathered from basalt — sticky red, fast-draining, and packed with minerals. That gives the durian grown here a drier, sweeter, richer flesh with a milder smell, enough to earn its own GI registration. This article walks you through which orchards let you come in and taste on the spot, when to go to catch the real thing, and roughly what you'll pay.

blocks.html: Volcanic durian isn't a new variety. Most of what's grown is Monthong, the same as the eastern provinces, but what people talk about is how the flavour shifts because of the soil. Grown on volcanic soil, the flesh comes out drier, crisp on the outside and soft within, sweet and rich without being cloying, and milder in smell than ordinary durian. Plenty of people who usually skip durian because of the smell can handle this one. It's the kind of thing you have to taste at the orchard to really get, because cut ripe off the tree and eaten fresh, it doesn't taste the same as fruit you buy and ripen at home.

blocks.text: When to go to catch the durian

blocks.html: Sisaket durian ripens quite a bit later than the eastern provinces. The main season runs roughly from late May to early July, with the peak — when fruit is plentiful and the most orchards are open — falling around mid-June. Depending on whether the rains come early or late in a given year, it can shift either way. If you're planning ahead, aim for mid-June first, then call the orchard to confirm before you set off, because early in the season fruit is still scarce, prices run high, and some farms aren't open to visitors yet.

blocks.title: Check before you go
blocks.html: Durian is a natural crop and no two years are alike. Before driving out a long way, call or message the orchard's Facebook/LINE to ask whether they have fruit right now and whether they're open for tasting in the orchard — so you don't make the trip for nothing.

blocks.html: Below are the orchards and volcanic-durian buying spots people actually visit in Kantharalak and Khun Han. Some are open farms you can walk through, with a café where you sit and eat in the orchard; others are farmers' stalls and storefronts selling freshly cut fruit. Prices are rough ranges and depend on grade and timing — pricey early in the season, cheaper mid-season.

items.name: Win Ka Va Farmhouse & Café
items.blurb: A volcanic-durian orchard that's also set up as a café in the grounds — walk among the trees, then sit and eat fresh durian with a drink all in one place. Good if you want the real orchard atmosphere rather than just buying to take away. It gets busy in season, so message the page to ask about availability first.

items.name: Wanarak Orchard
items.blurb: A Kantharalak orchard selling direct from the farm, with volcanic Monthong at friendlier prices than many. The focus is on fruit cut fully ripe — if you want durian to actually eat rather than photograph, this one's good value.

items.name: Mae Si Chan Volcanic Durian Orchard
items.blurb: A Kantharalak orchard with both volcanic durian and rambutan, selling at the farm gate during the season — handy for picking up several things in one stop. The rambutan here is grown on the same volcanic soil.

items.name: Chok Mueang Si Volcanic Durian Orchard
items.blurb: A well-known orchard in Khun Han selling freshly cut, graded fruit. Prices run a touch higher because they control quality — good if you want nice-looking durian with firm flesh that you can give as a gift without worry.

items.name: Bun Song Orchard
items.blurb: A Khun Han orchard with clearly separated grades — premium and quality grades at different prices, and they tell you exactly what you get for what you pay. Good if you want to choose by budget. Cut fresh from the farm.

items.name: Phaiboon Health Orchard
items.blurb: One of the sellers under the Lava Durian network, selling volcanic Monthong with a focus on farm standards — cut ripe and shipped direct. Good if you want fruit with a clearly certified growing origin.

items.name: Ta Toem Orchard
items.blurb: A small orchard that reviewers stop by to taste often, with a genuine village-farm feel — the owner walks you among the trees and tells you about the volcanic soil. There isn't much fruit, so go when there's stock to find it.

items.name: Lung Khammi Orchard
items.blurb: Another small orchard often paired with Ta Toem in reviews, selling fruit from its own trees. You can chat with the owner, prices follow the season, and it's good for anyone who likes supporting small-scale growers.

items.name: Roadside stalls along the Khun Han–Kantharalak route
items.blurb: In season, farmers set up stalls along the main roads in and out of the growing area — prices are negotiable and the selection is varied, but you need to know what you're doing. Pick a vendor who can tell you which orchard it's from and lets you taste before you buy.

blocks.title: How to buy without getting it wrong
blocks.html: Always ask to taste first. Durian ripened just right has flesh that's soft but not mushy, sweet and rich without bitterness — if a vendor won't let you taste at all, be wary. · Ask how many days ago it was cut; if you want to eat it that same day, pick a fruit that's just starting to smell. · If you're hauling it a long way, choose fruit that's fully mature but not yet fully ripe, and let it finish ripening yourself.

blocks.text: Why volcanic soil changes the flavour

blocks.html: The growing area sits on the foothills of the Phanom Dong Rak range, which once had ancient volcanoes. The soil here weathered from basalt into red clay that drains very well and is rich in nutrients. The result is durian trees that don't sit waterlogged, roots that don't rot easily, and full mineral uptake — so the flesh comes out drier, an even yellow, sweet and rich and firm rather than mushy. That's why the same Monthong variety, grown in Sisaket versus elsewhere, doesn't taste the same.

items: Dry, firm flesh — not mushy; holds its shape when you scoop it
Sweet and rich, not cloying — just sweet enough, with a creamy finish
Milder smell than usual — many who fear durian's smell can eat this one
Thin husk, lots of flesh — good flesh-to-fruit value
A GI product — registered to a specific origin; grown only in these 3 districts

blocks.html: Every year the province holds the Sisaket Volcanic Durian Festival from mid to late June, in front of the provincial hall, bringing orchards from across the area together in one place. There's an air-conditioned fruit market where you can taste and buy volcanic Monthong durian, rambutan, mangosteen, OTOP products and local specialities. In 2025 it ran 19–23 June; future dates shift with the season. If you'd rather not drive around hunting for orchards one by one, this is the one stop that has it all.

blocks.title: If you can't make the festival dates
blocks.html: Many orchards ship volcanic durian online direct from the farm — choose from the Lava Durian network or a trustworthy orchard page. But once you're actually in Sisaket, tasting it fresh in the orchard beats it every time.

The orchards are spread across Kantharalak, Khun Han and Si Rattana, and driving between districts takes a fair while. It's better to pick one zone per day and pair it with nearby sights than to crisscross districts all day.

faq.q: When is Sisaket volcanic durian in season?
faq.a: The main season runs roughly from late May to early July, with the most fruit and the most open orchards around mid-June. It shifts year to year with the rains, so call the orchard to confirm before you travel.

faq.q: How much does volcanic durian cost per kilo?
faq.a: It depends on grade and timing, but generally around 180–250 THB per kilo. Premium grades cost more, prices run high early in the season and drop mid-season, and buying at the farm gate usually gets you a better price.

faq.q: How is volcanic durian different from ordinary durian?
faq.a: Most of it is the same Monthong variety, but grown on old volcanic soil that drains well and is rich in nutrients, which makes the flesh drier and firmer, sweet and rich without being cloying, and milder in smell.

faq.q: Which districts is it grown in?
faq.a: The main GI-registered growing areas are Kantharalak, Khun Han and Si Rattana, all on the volcanic-soil foothills of the Phanom Dong Rak range.

faq.q: How do I buy it if I can't visit in season?
faq.a: Many orchards ship online direct from the farm — choose from the Lava Durian network or an orchard page that's clear about its growing origin. Still, the flavour of fruit eaten fresh in the orchard is different from fruit ripened at home.
